sections.title: NBME BLUEPRINT & TWO-STEP LOGIC
sections.body:
Target Concept: Hematology — Hypercoagulable states / Thrombophilia

Core Mechanism: Factor V Leiden is a point mutation (Arg506Gln) that makes Factor V resistant to inactivation by activated Protein C. This is the most common inherited thrombophilia (~5% of Caucasians). Combined with immobilization (long flight), it dramatically increases DVT/PE risk.

Multi-Step Logic:

[Step 1] SOB + tachycardia + hypoxemia + clear lungs

→ Pulmonary embolism

[Step 2] Right calf swelling + tenderness

→ DVT as source

[Step 3] Young woman + prolonged immobilization

→ Inherited thrombophilia?

[Step 4] Most common inherited cause of DVT/PE

→ Factor V Leiden mutation ✓

sections.title: NBME BLUEPRINT & TWO-STEP LOGIC
sections.body:
Target Concept: Neurology — Brainstem syndromes / Medial pontine syndrome (Foville syndrome variant)

Core Mechanism: The lesion is in the left medial pons, affecting:

Left MLF → internuclear ophthalmoplegia (left eye can't adduct on rightward gaze — wait, re-reading: left eye stays midline on LEFT gaze, meaning the RIGHT eye should be abducting and left eye should adduct but doesn't). Actually: on looking LEFT, right eye adducts and left eye remains midline → this means the LEFT abducens nucleus or nerve is affected (left eye can't abduct on left gaze). Plus the right eye adducts normally. This is actually a left CN VI palsy, not INO.

Re-analysis: On right gaze → right eye abducts, left eye adducts (normal). On left gaze → right eye adducts, left eye remains midline (can't abduct). This = left lateral rectus palsy = left CN VI lesion.

Right hemiparesis = left corticospinal tract (before decussation in medulla)

Right decreased vibration/2-point discrimination = left medial lemniscus

This is medial pontine syndrome (left side): CN VI + corticospinal tract + medial lemniscus

The left CN VII nucleus is also in the pons near CN VI → left facial nerve palsy → asymmetric smile (LMN facial weakness on left = entire left face droops)

Multi-Step Logic:

[Step 1] Left eye can't abduct on left gaze

→ Left CN VI palsy

[Step 2] Right hemiparesis + right sensory loss

→ Left-sided brainstem lesion

(corticospinal tract + medial lemniscus)

[Step 3] Localize: Left medial pons

→ CN VI + CN VII nuclei are neighbors

[Step 4] CN VII involvement → LMN facial palsy

→ Asymmetric smile ✓

sections.body:
Target Concept: Infectious Disease — Acute HIV seroconversion (acute retroviral syndrome)

Core Mechanism: Acute HIV infection presents 2–4 weeks after exposure with a mononucleosis-like syndrome: fever, pharyngitis, diffuse lymphadenopathy, rash. The critical distinguishing feature is pancytopenia (HIV directly infects CD4+ T cells and bone marrow progenitors) and a negative heterophile antibody test (ruling out EBV mono).

[Step 1] Fever + pharyngitis + diffuse LAD

→ Mono-like syndrome

[Step 2] Heterophile antibody NEGATIVE

→ NOT EBV mononucleosis

[Step 3] PANCYTOPENIA (low Hgb, WBC, Plt)

→ Bone marrow suppression

[Step 4] Mono-like illness + negative heterophile

         + pancytopenia in young adult

→ Acute HIV seroconversion ✓

sections.title: NBME BLUEPRINT & TWO-STEP LOGIC
sections.body:
Target Concept: Renal Pathology — Acute Interstitial Nephritis (AIN) / Drug-induced hypersensitivity

Core Mechanism: AIN is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction to drugs (commonly β-lactams like oxacillin, NSAIDs, sulfonamides). The interstitium is infiltrated by eosinophils, lymphocytes, and macrophages, causing tubular damage. Classic triad: fever + rash + eosinophilia with acute renal failure and urine eosinophils.

Multi-Step Logic:

→ Drug exposure

[Step 2] New fever + maculopapular rash + eosinophilia

→ Drug hypersensitivity reaction

[Step 3] Acute renal failure (Cr 5.7, BUN 65)

         + urine eosinophils + WBC casts

→ Acute interstitial nephritis

[Step 4] Pathology = interstitial inflammatory

infiltrate (eosinophils + lymphocytes) ✓

sections.title: VIGNETTE CLUES & PATTERN-RECOGNITION
sections.body:
Diagnostic Anchors:

🔑 Central syrinx on cervical MRI = syringomyelia

🔑 Bilateral upper extremity weakness + decreased pinprick = "cape-like" distribution (crossing anterior white commissure fibers destroyed)

🔑 Young patient → ask about trauma (post-traumatic syrinx) or Chiari malformation

The "Hack": Syringomyelia + "additional history" = trauma or Chiari. Since Chiari isn't a history question (it's imaging), trauma is the answer.

The Reversal: Diet (A) → nutritional deficiency causes peripheral neuropathy, not central syrinx. Family illness (B) → no hereditary syrinx pattern. Travel (C) → infections cause myelitis, not cystic syrinx. Weight loss (E) → suggests malignancy, but tumor would appear as a mass, not a syrinx.

sections.title: SYSTEMATIC DISTRACTOR EXPOSURE
sections.body:

A) Diet	Nutritional deficiency (B₁₂) causing subacute combined degeneration	B₁₂ deficiency affects posterior columns + lateral corticospinal tracts, NOT a central syrinx.
B) Family illness	Hereditary condition (e.g., hereditary spastic paraplegia)	Syringomyelia is not inherited. No familial pattern.
C) Recent travel	Infectious myelitis (e.g., schistosomiasis, TB)	Infections cause transverse myelitis with inflammation, not a cystic syrinx cavity.
E) Unintended weight loss	Intramedullary spinal cord tumor (e.g., ependymoma, astrocytoma)	Tumors appear as enhancing masses on MRI, not a simple syrinx. Though tumors CAN cause syrinx, the question says "central syrinx" — trauma is the more direct historical question.

✅ Correct Answer: (B) Cimetidine = B, Omeprazole = A

sections.title: 🔑 VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Cimetidine = H₂ receptor antagonist → partial acid suppression → pH rises moderately

🔑 Omeprazole = proton pump inhibitor → near-complete acid suppression → pH rises maximally

🔑 Curve interpretation: Omeprazole produces the HIGHEST pH (most acid suppression) = Curve A (highest). Cimetidine produces moderate pH elevation = Curve B.

🧠 MULTI-STEP LOGIC

[Step 1] Omeprazole = PPI = IRREVERSIBLE inhibition of H⁺/K⁺ ATPase

→ Maximum acid suppression → Highest pH curve = A

[Step 2] Cimetidine = H₂ blocker = REVERSIBLE competitive antagonist

→ Partial acid suppression → Moderate pH curve = B

[Step 3] Match: Cimetidine = B, Omeprazole = A ✓

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
All other combinations either assign the wrong potency ranking (PPIs > H₂ blockers for acid suppression) or reverse the curves. The key rule: PPI always produces greater pH elevation than H₂ blocker.

sections.title: 🔑 VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Right colon cancer → drains via superior mesenteric vein → portal vein → LIVER (first site of metastasis)

🔑 Liver metastases already present → cancer then enters hepatic veins → IVC → right heart → LUNGS

🔑 Question asks how cancer reached the lungs (not the liver)

🧠 MULTI-STEP LOGIC

[Step 1] Right colon → superior mesenteric vein → portal vein → LIVER

(explains liver mets)

[Step 2] Liver → hepatic veins → INFERIOR VENA CAVA → right heart → lungs

(explains lung mets)

[Step 3] The structure connecting liver to lungs = IVC ✓

D) Middle colic artery	Never — arteries don't carry metastases in this direction	Cancer spreads via VEINS, not arteries.
E) Pulmonary vein	Cancer were already in the lungs spreading to systemic circulation	Pulmonary veins carry blood FROM lungs TO left heart — wrong direction.
F) Superior mesenteric artery	Never — arteries supply, not drain	Same as D — wrong vessel type.
G) Superior vena cava	Cancer were from head/neck/upper extremity	Right colon → liver → hepatic veins → IVC (not SVC).

18.stemSnippet: 18-year-old woman with sickle cell disease… RUQ pain radiating to right shoulder… gallstones on ultrasound. Most likely underlying cause?

sections.title: Snapshot
sections.body:
18-year-old woman with sickle cell disease… RUQ pain radiating to right shoulder… gallstones on ultrasound. Most likely underlying cause?

✅ Correct Answer: E) Overload of unconjugated bilirubin

sections.title: 🔑 VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Sickle cell disease → chronic hemolytic anemia → excess unconjugated bilirubin

🔑 Unconjugated bilirubin is conjugated in liver → excreted in bile → but excess bilirubin overwhelms the system

🔑 Excess bilirubin in bile → calcium bilirubinate (pigment) gallstones

🔑 RUQ pain radiating to right shoulder = biliary colic (phrenic nerve irritation)

🧠 MULTI-STEP LOGIC

[Step 1] Sickle cell disease → chronic hemolysis

[Step 2] Hemolysis → ↑ unconjugated bilirubin

[Step 3] ↑ Bilirubin → ↑ conjugated bilirubin in bile

[Step 4] Excess bilirubin precipitates → PIGMENT stones

(calcium bilirubinate = BLACK stones)

[Step 5] Underlying cause = bilirubin overload ✓

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Would Be Correct If…	Dealbreaker
A) Decreased hepatic secretion of lecithin	Lecithin deficiency → cholesterol precipitation → cholesterol stones	No evidence of lecithin deficiency. Sickle cell = pigment stones, not cholesterol.
B) Decreased reabsorption of bile salts	Ileal disease (Crohn's) → bile salt wasting → cholesterol stones	No GI disease mentioned. Sickle cell = hemolysis = pigment stones.
C) High cholesterol:bile acid ratio	Obesity, estrogen, or metabolic syndrome → cholesterol supersaturation	Cholesterol stones are the most common overall, but in sickle cell, the mechanism is bilirubin overload.
D) Parasites secreting β-glucuronidase	Clonorchis sinensis or Ascaris infection → deconjugation of bilirubin → brown pigment stones	No travel history or parasite exposure. Brown pigment stones = infection. Black pigment stones = hemolysis.

✅ Correct Answer: D) Proto-oncogene

sections.title: 🔑 VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Pheochromocytoma (history) + parathyroid tumor (mother) + parafollicular cell neoplasm (medullary thyroid carcinoma) = MEN 2A

🔑 Parafollicular cells = C cells → produce calcitonin → medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC)

🔑 Diarrhea = caused by calcitonin secretion from MTC

🔑 MEN 2A is caused by gain-of-function mutation in RET proto-oncogene (chromosome 10)

🧠 MULTI-STEP LOGIC

[Step 1] Pheochromocytoma + parathyroid tumor + MTC

→ MEN 2A syndrome

[Step 2] MEN 2A = RET proto-oncogene mutation

[Step 3] RET = receptor tyrosine kinase

→ Gain-of-function = proto-oncogene ✓

[Step 4] Proto-oncogene (not tumor suppressor)

because it's a GAIN-of-function mutation

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS

E) Tumor suppressor gene	Tumor had LOSS-of-function mutation (e.g., MEN 1 = menin gene)	MEN 1 = tumor suppressor (menin). MEN 2 = proto-oncogene (RET). Critical distinction!

Newborn… 36 weeks… ambiguous genitalia… Na⁺ 133 (low), K⁺ 5.0 (high-normal), HCO₃⁻ 17 (low), Glucose 42.

✅ Correct Answer: B) Aldosterone receptor

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Ambiguous genitalia → disorder of sexual development → excess androgens in XX or deficient androgens in XY

🔑 Hyponatremia (133) + Hyperkalemia (5.0) + Metabolic acidosis (HCO₃⁻ 17) = aldosterone deficiency (salt-wasting)

🔑 Hypoglycemia (42) = cortisol deficiency

🔑 Combined cortisol + aldosterone deficiency + ambiguous genitalia = Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency)

🔑 Treatment = replace cortisol (glucocorticoid) + fludrocortisone (mineralocorticoid = aldosterone receptor agonist)

🧠 MULTI-STEP LOGIC

[Step 1] Ambiguous genitalia + salt-wasting (↓Na, ↑K)

→ Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH)

[Step 2] Most common CAH = 21-hydroxylase deficiency

→ Cannot make cortisol or aldosterone

→ Shunts precursors to androgens

[Step 3] Treatment targets:

→ Glucocorticoid receptor (hydrocortisone)

→ ALDOSTERONE receptor (fludrocortisone) ✓

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Would Be Correct If…	Dealbreaker
A) ACTH receptor	Treating ACTH deficiency (secondary adrenal insufficiency)	ACTH is already HIGH in CAH (driving the hyperplasia). You don't target ACTH receptors.
C) Androgen receptor	Treating androgen excess with an anti-androgen (e.g., flutamide)	Anti-androgens may be adjunctive later, but the ACUTE life-threatening issue is salt-wasting → aldosterone replacement is priority.
D) GnRH receptor	Treating central precocious puberty with leuprolide	No precocious puberty here. This is a newborn with salt-wasting crisis.
E) Growth hormone receptor	Treating GH deficiency	No growth issue in a newborn. The acute problem is electrolyte crisis.
IF ambiguous genitalia + hyponatremia + hyperkalemia in newborn → THEN CAH (21-hydroxylase deficiency) → treat with fludrocortisone (targets aldosterone receptor)

✅ Correct Answer: E) Spleen

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Left posterior 10th intercostal space = anatomic location overlying the spleen (ribs 9-11 on left)

🔑 Hemorrhagic shock (tachycardia, hypotension, pale/cold/clammy) = solid organ injury with significant bleeding

🔑 Spleen is the most commonly injured abdominal organ in trauma and is highly vascular

🧠 MULTI-STEP LOGIC

[Step 1] Entry wound: left posterior 10th intercostal space

→ Overlies the spleen (left upper quadrant, ribs 9-11)

[Step 2] Signs of hemorrhagic shock

→ Solid organ bleeding (spleen is most vascular)

[Step 3] CT would show splenic laceration/hematoma ✓

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Would Be Correct If…	Dealbreaker
A) Adrenal gland	Wound were more medial/superior and retroperitoneal	Adrenal glands are small, deep, and retroperitoneal — unlikely target from this entry point.
B) Colon	Wound were more anterior/inferior	Splenic flexure of colon is nearby but the posterior 10th ICS on left directly overlies the spleen.
C) Kidney	Wound were more posterior/medial at the costovertebral angle	Left kidney is more medial and posterior. The 10th ICS laterally/posteriorly = spleen territory.
D) Lung	Wound caused pneumothorax with respiratory symptoms	The 10th ICS is below the lung base posteriorly. Also, hemorrhagic shock suggests abdominal solid organ, not lung.
IF penetrating trauma to left posterior 10th ICS + hemorrhagic shock → THEN spleen injury

27.stemSnippet: 33-year-old man… psychiatric admission 5 days ago… olanzapine + clonazepam started… now fever 40.3°C, tachycardia, hypertension, tachypnea. Physical exam most likely shows?

sections.title: Snapshot
sections.body:
33-year-old man… psychiatric admission 5 days ago… olanzapine + clonazepam started… now fever 40.3°C, tachycardia, hypertension, tachypnea. Physical exam most likely shows?

✅ Correct Answer: B) Muscle rigidity

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Olanzapine = antipsychotic (dopamine D₂ antagonist)

🔑 5 days after starting antipsychotic = classic timeline for Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS)

🔑 High fever (40.3°C) + tachycardia + hypertension + tachypnea = autonomic instability

🔑 Confusion/agitation preceded the fever = altered mental status

🔑 NMS classic tetrad: Fever + Rigidity + Autonomic instability + Altered mental status

🧠 MULTI-STEP LOGIC

[Step 1] Antipsychotic (olanzapine) started recently

→ Risk for NMS

[Step 2] High fever + autonomic instability + AMS

→ 3 of 4 NMS criteria present

[Step 3] Missing finding on exam = MUSCLE RIGIDITY ✓

("lead-pipe" rigidity)

[Step 4] NMS tetrad complete: FARM

F = Fever

A = Autonomic instability

R = Rigidity ✓

M = Mental status changes

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Would Be Correct If…	Dealbreaker
A) Hyperreflexia	Patient had SEROTONIN SYNDROME (SSRIs, MAOIs)	Serotonin syndrome = hyperreflexia + CLONUS + myoclonus. NMS = RIGIDITY (not hyperreflexia). Key distinguisher!
C) Mydriasis	Patient had anticholinergic toxicity or sympathomimetic overdose	NMS doesn't typically cause mydriasis. Pupils are usually normal in NMS.
D) Petechial rash	Patient had meningococcemia, DIC, or thrombocytopenia	No infectious or hematologic cause suggested. Antipsychotic + fever = NMS.
E) Unilateral hemiparesis	Patient had a stroke	No focal neurologic deficits in NMS. This is a diffuse process.

28.stemSnippet: 68-year-old man… painless hematuria × 3 months… retired lab technician (naphthylamine exposure)… smokes 1.5 ppd × 45 years… CT: mass in pelvis of left kidney. Neoplasm type?

✅ Correct Answer: E) Urothelial carcinoma

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Naphthylamine exposure = aromatic amine = classic occupational carcinogen for urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma

🔑 Heavy smoking = additional major risk factor for urothelial carcinoma

🔑 Mass in renal PELVIS (not renal parenchyma) = urothelial lining, not renal cortex

🔑 Painless hematuria = classic presentation of urinary tract malignancy

🧠 MULTI-STEP LOGIC

[Step 1] Painless hematuria + mass in renal pelvis

→ Urinary tract neoplasm

[Step 2] Renal PELVIS = lined by urothelium (transitional epithelium)

→ Urothelial carcinoma

[Step 3] Risk factors confirm:

├─ Smoking ✓

└─ Both are #1 and #2 risk factors for urothelial CA

C) Nephroblastoma	Child <5 years with large abdominal mass (Wilms tumor)	Nephroblastoma is a PEDIATRIC tumor. This is a 68-year-old man.
D) Oncocytoma	Incidental well-circumscribed renal cortical mass with central scar	Oncocytomas are benign cortical tumors, not in the renal pelvis. Not associated with carcinogen exposure.

[Step 2] Common rosacea triggers:

├─ Alcohol (especially red wine) ✓

├─ Spicy foods

B) Excessive sweating	Suspecting pheochromocytoma or carcinoid syndrome	No episodic hypertension, palpitations, or diarrhea. Facial redness pattern = rosacea, not carcinoid flushing.

30.stemSnippet: 5-year-old girl… never vaccinated… mother declines all vaccines… child has never had a vaccine-preventable illness. Most likely explanation for good health?

sections.title: Snapshot
sections.body:
5-year-old girl… never vaccinated… mother declines all vaccines… child has never had a vaccine-preventable illness. Most likely explanation for good health?

✅ Correct Answer: B) Herd immunity

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Unvaccinated child who has never been sick with vaccine-preventable illness

🔑 Lives in a community where most others are vaccinated

🔑 Herd immunity = when a sufficient proportion of the population is immune, the unvaccinated are indirectly protected because disease transmission is interrupted

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Would Be Correct If…	Dealbreaker
A) Community eradication	The diseases were completely eradicated (like smallpox)	Most vaccine-preventable diseases (measles, pertussis, etc.) are NOT eradicated — they still circulate.
C) Lingering maternal antibodies	Child were <6 months old	Maternal IgG wanes by 6 months. This child is 5 years old — no maternal antibody protection remains.
D) Normal immune system	A normal immune system alone prevented infection	A normal immune system helps fight infection but doesn't prevent EXPOSURE. Without vaccination, exposure would eventually lead to infection without herd immunity.
E) Underdiagnosis	Subclinical infections were missed	Possible but not the MOST LIKELY explanation. Herd immunity is the primary reason unvaccinated children in vaccinated communities stay healthy.
IF unvaccinated child healthy in vaccinated community → THEN herd immunity

31.stemSnippet: 28-year-old woman, G2P1… Rh-negative… husband Rh-positive… first child delivered vaginally… indirect Coombs titer 1:32 after delivery… now 12 weeks pregnant. Pharmacotherapy mechanism?

sections.title: Snapshot
sections.body:
28-year-old woman, G2P1… Rh-negative… husband Rh-positive… first child delivered vaginally… indirect Coombs titer 1:32 after delivery… now 12 weeks pregnant. Pharmacotherapy mechanism?

✅ Correct Answer: A) Binding to the D antigen on fetal erythrocytes

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Rh-negative mother + Rh-positive father = risk for hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN)

🔑 Indirect Coombs 1:32 after first delivery = mother was ALREADY sensitized (has anti-D antibodies)

🔑 Second pregnancy = fetus at risk for HDN from maternal anti-D IgG crossing placenta

🔑 RhoGAM (anti-D immunoglobulin) = binds to D antigen on fetal RBCs that entered maternal circulation → prevents further maternal sensitization

🧠 MULTI-STEP LOGIC

[Step 1] Rh-negative mother + Rh-positive fetus

→ Risk of alloimmunization

[Step 2] Already sensitized (Coombs 1:32)

→ Anti-D antibodies present

[Step 3] RhoGAM mechanism:

→ Anti-D IgG BINDS to D antigen on fetal RBCs

→ Opsonizes them for splenic removal

→ Prevents maternal B cells from "seeing" the antigen

→ Prevents FURTHER antibody production ✓

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Would Be Correct If…	Dealbreaker
B) Blockade of complement binding	RhoGAM worked by preventing complement-mediated hemolysis	RhoGAM works by opsonization/clearance, not complement blockade.
C) Induction of class switching	Treatment changed antibody isotype	RhoGAM doesn't induce class switching — it prevents immune recognition.
D) Inhibition of fetal blood group A erythrocyte production	Treatment suppressed fetal erythropoiesis	RhoGAM doesn't affect fetal RBC production. It targets D antigen on fetal cells in maternal circulation.
E) Prevention of fetal RBCs from entering maternal circulation	A physical barrier existed	RhoGAM doesn't prevent fetomaternal hemorrhage — it clears fetal RBCs AFTER they enter maternal blood.
IF Rh-negative mother + Rh-positive fetus → THEN RhoGAM → mechanism = binds D antigen on fetal RBCs

✅ Correct Answer: A) "Do you have any concerns about your alcohol use?"

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 DUI citation = red flag for problematic alcohol use

🔑 "Drank a bit more than usual" = minimizing language

🔑 Records say "drinks socially" = may be underreported

🔑 Question asks for initial response = screen, don't assume

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS

B) "How has your alcohol use been this week compared to last week…"	Assumes ongoing problematic use without first exploring the patient's own perspective. Skips the screening step.
C) "So you're here because you're concerned about your alcohol use…"	Puts words in the patient's mouth. She came for a routine exam, not for alcohol concerns. Presumptive.
D) "When was your last drink?"	Appropriate for detox assessment but premature here. Need to first explore whether the patient perceives a problem.
E) "Would you be willing to go through a detoxification program?"	Massively premature. Jumps to treatment before any assessment. Assumes alcohol dependence without evidence.

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES

D) Neural crest	Gives rise to melanocytes, PNS ganglia, adrenal medulla, craniofacial bones. Not lymphatics.
E) Neuroectoderm	Gives rise to CNS neurons, retina, posterior pituitary. Not lymphatics.

35.stemSnippet: 50-year-old man… obstructive sleep apnea… BMI 63… gray-blue lips/earlobes/nails… pH 7.31, PCO₂ 70, PO₂ 50. Most likely additional finding?

sections.title: Snapshot
sections.body:
50-year-old man… obstructive sleep apnea… BMI 63… gray-blue lips/earlobes/nails… pH 7.31, PCO₂ 70, PO₂ 50. Most likely additional finding?

✅ Correct Answer: B) Increased hemoglobin concentration

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Morbid obesity (BMI 63) + OSA + daytime somnolence = Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (OHS / Pickwickian syndrome)

🔑 Cyanosis (gray-blue lips/earlobes/nails) = chronic hypoxemia

🔑 ABG: pH 7.31, PCO₂ 70, PO₂ 50 = chronic respiratory acidosis with hypoxemia and hypercapnia

🔑 Chronic hypoxemia → EPO release → secondary polycythemia → ↑ hemoglobin

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
A) Decreased serum bicarbonate	Chronic respiratory acidosis causes INCREASED (not decreased) bicarb as renal compensation.
C) Increased total lung capacity	OHS causes DECREASED TLC due to obesity restricting chest wall expansion. Increased TLC = emphysema.
D) Left ventricular hypertrophy	Chronic hypoxemia → pulmonary vasoconstriction → pulmonary HTN → RIGHT ventricular hypertrophy (cor pulmonale), not left.
IF chronic hypoxemia (any cause) → THEN secondary polycythemia → ↑ hemoglobin

36.stemSnippet: 5-year-old girl… bloody diarrhea → 5 days later: decreased urine output, HTN, pallor… Hgb 8.5, Plt 45,000, Cr 3.3. Most likely infectious agent?

sections.title: Snapshot
sections.body:
5-year-old girl… bloody diarrhea → 5 days later: decreased urine output, HTN, pallor… Hgb 8.5, Plt 45,000, Cr 3.3. Most likely infectious agent?

✅ Correct Answer: B) Escherichia coli

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Bloody diarrhea → then anemia + thrombocytopenia + renal failure = Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS)

🔑 HUS triad: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia + Thrombocytopenia + Acute renal failure

🔑 Classic cause = E. coli O157:H7 (Shiga toxin-producing / STEC)

🔑 Child with diarrhea-associated HUS = textbook STEC-HUS

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
A) Campylobacter jejuni	Causes bloody diarrhea but associated with Guillain-Barré syndrome, not HUS.
C) Rotavirus	Causes WATERY (not bloody) diarrhea in infants. Doesn't cause HUS.
D) Salmonella enterica	Causes bloody diarrhea but associated with osteomyelitis (sickle cell) and reactive arthritis, not HUS.
E) Yersinia pestis	Causes plague (bubonic, pneumonic). Not associated with diarrhea or HUS.
IF bloody diarrhea → HUS (anemia + thrombocytopenia + renal failure) in a child → THEN E. coli O157:H7

37.stemSnippet: 52-year-old woman… headaches… BP 154/100… PMI displaced left… occasional skipped beats… ECG: left axis deviation, R waves >30mm in V5-V6. Process explaining LV abnormalities?

sections.title: Snapshot
sections.body:
52-year-old woman… headaches… BP 154/100… PMI displaced left… occasional skipped beats… ECG: left axis deviation, R waves >30mm in V5-V6. Process explaining LV abnormalities?

✅ Correct Answer: C) Increased synthesis of contractile filaments

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Chronic hypertension (154/100)

🔑 PMI displaced left = LV enlargement

🔑 ECG: left axis deviation + tall R waves in V5-V6 = LV hypertrophy (LVH)

🔑 LVH from pressure overload → concentric hypertrophy → sarcomeres added in parallel → increased synthesis of contractile filaments (actin/myosin)

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
A) Excessive glycogen accumulation	Seen in glycogen storage diseases (Pompe disease). Not caused by hypertension.
B) Fibrosis of conduction pathways	Would cause conduction blocks/arrhythmias, not hypertrophy. Fibrosis ≠ hypertrophy.
D) Misfolding/aggregation of cytoskeletal proteins	Seen in amyloidosis or certain cardiomyopathies. Not the mechanism of pressure-overload hypertrophy.
E) Myocyte hyperplasia from embryonic genes	Adult cardiomyocytes undergo HYPERTROPHY (cell enlargement), not hyperplasia (cell division). Cardiac myocytes are terminally differentiated.
IF chronic HTN + LVH on ECG → THEN pressure overload → increased contractile filament synthesis (sarcomeres in parallel)

38.stemSnippet: Investigator studying lung cancer risk… benzene exposure + smoking… SNPs in metabolic activation enzymes increase cancer risk. Which enzyme?

sections.title: Snapshot
sections.body:
Investigator studying lung cancer risk… benzene exposure + smoking… SNPs in metabolic activation enzymes increase cancer risk. Which enzyme?

✅ Correct Answer: B) Cytochrome P450

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Metabolic ACTIVATION = Phase I metabolism = cytochrome P450

🔑 P450 enzymes convert procarcinogens → active carcinogens (electrophilic metabolites that damage DNA)

🔑 Benzene and tobacco smoke contain procarcinogens activated by CYP450

🔑 SNPs in CYP450 genes → variable activation rates → variable cancer risk

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
A) Aldehyde dehydrogenase	Metabolizes acetaldehyde (alcohol metabolism). Not involved in carcinogen activation.
C) Glutathione S-transferase	Phase II DETOXIFICATION enzyme. Conjugates reactive metabolites for excretion. Polymorphisms here would affect detox, not activation.
D) Methyltransferase	Involved in DNA methylation/epigenetics. Not a Phase I activating enzyme.
E) Succinate dehydrogenase	TCA cycle enzyme (Complex II). Not involved in xenobiotic metabolism.
IF "metabolic activation" of procarcinogens → THEN cytochrome P450 (Phase I)

39.stemSnippet: New malaria drug… assessing maximum tolerated dose + pharmacokinetics in 80 healthy volunteers. Which phase?

sections.title: Snapshot
sections.body:
New malaria drug… assessing maximum tolerated dose + pharmacokinetics in 80 healthy volunteers. Which phase?

✅ Correct Answer: B) Phase 1

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Healthy volunteers (not patients with disease)

🔑 Maximum tolerated dose = dose-finding / safety

🔑 Pharmacokinetics = absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion

🔑 Small sample (80) = Phase 1

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS

E) [(1.2/100) − (1.8/100)] / (1.8/100) — This is RELATIVE risk reduction (RRR), not ARR; also reversed.

sections.body: IF asked for ARR → THEN subtract: Risk(control) − Risk(treatment)

69.stemSnippet: 5-year-old boy… bed-wetting 2-3x/week… daytime continence achieved at age 3.5… never achieved nighttime continence… no fever, polydipsia, dysuria, constipation… normal exam + normal urinalysis. Most likely cause?

5-year-old boy… bed-wetting 2-3x/week… daytime continence achieved at age 3.5… never achieved nighttime continence… no fever, polydipsia, dysuria, constipation… normal exam + normal urinalysis. Most likely cause?

✅ Correct Answer: C) Delayed maturation of detrusor and sphincter control

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Primary nocturnal enuresis = never achieved nighttime dryness (vs secondary = was dry then relapsed)

🔑 Age 5 = still within normal developmental range for nighttime continence

🔑 Normal exam + normal UA = no structural, infectious, or metabolic cause

🔑 No red flags (no polydipsia → no diabetes insipidus; no dysuria → no UTI; no constipation)

🔑 Most common cause = developmental delay in bladder maturation — the child's nervous system hasn't yet developed full nocturnal bladder control

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
A) Abnormal insertion of terminal ureter	= Ectopic ureter. Would cause CONTINUOUS dribbling (not just nocturnal). More common in girls.
B) Bladder colonization / recurrent UTI	UA is NORMAL. No dysuria or fever. No evidence of infection.
D) Occult neurologic lesion	Neurologic exam is normal. No bowel dysfunction. No sacral dimple or other signs of spinal dysraphism.
E) Vesicoureteral reflux	VUR causes recurrent UTIs, not isolated nocturnal enuresis. UA is normal.
IF primary nocturnal enuresis + normal exam + normal UA + age ≤7 → THEN delayed maturation of detrusor/sphincter control

70.stemSnippet: 5-year-old boy… bloody stool (hard "like pebbles") + bright red blood on tissue… previous BM was 5 days ago… rectal exam: 1 cm bright red rectal mucosa protruding from right side of anus. Most likely cause of physical findings?

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Hard, pebble-like stools = constipation

🔑 5 days between bowel movements = infrequent stools

🔑 Bright red blood on tissue = anal/rectal source (not upper GI)

🔑 1 cm bright red rectal mucosa protruding = rectal prolapse

🔑 Constipation with chronic straining → rectal prolapse in children

🔑 Height 5th percentile, weight 10th percentile = small but BMI 50th percentile (proportionate)

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
B) Cystic fibrosis	CF CAN cause rectal prolapse (from malabsorption + bulky stools), but this child has CONSTIPATION (hard stools), not the bulky/greasy stools of CF. No respiratory symptoms.
C) Hirschsprung disease	Hirschsprung presents in infancy with failure to pass meconium, abdominal distension. By age 5 with normal prior history, this is unlikely.
D) Hookworm infestation	Hookworm causes iron deficiency anemia, not constipation or rectal prolapse. No travel history.
E) Intussusception	Presents with "currant jelly" stools, colicky abdominal pain, sausage-shaped mass. Not hard pebble stools.
IF child + hard infrequent stools + straining + rectal prolapse → THEN constipation

71.stemSnippet: 27-year-old nulligravid woman (III-5 in pedigree)… brother has cystic fibrosis… wants to know her risk of being a CF carrier. Best approximation?

sections.title: Snapshot
sections.body:
27-year-old nulligravid woman (III-5 in pedigree)… brother has cystic fibrosis… wants to know her risk of being a CF carrier. Best approximation?

✅ Correct Answer: D) 2 of 3

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Cystic fibrosis = autosomal recessive

🔑 Brother has CF → both parents are carriers (Aa × Aa)

🔑 Possible offspring genotypes: AA (1/4), Aa (2/4), aa (1/4)

🔑 She does NOT have CF (she's healthy) → she is either AA or Aa

🔑 Among unaffected siblings: probability of being a carrier = 2/3

🧠 MULTI-STEP LOGIC

[Step 1] Both parents are carriers (Aa × Aa)

[Step 2] Offspring possibilities:

AA = 1/4 (25%)

Aa = 2/4 (50%) ← carrier

aa = 1/4 (25%) ← affected (CF)

[Step 3] She is UNAFFECTED → eliminate aa

[Step 4] Among unaffected (AA + Aa):

AA = 1/3

Aa = 2/3 ✓

[Step 5] Probability she is a carrier = 2/3

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
A) 1 of 2	This would be the carrier probability if we didn't know the brother had CF (general population carrier frequency consideration).
B) 1 of 3	This is the probability of being homozygous NORMAL (AA) among unaffected siblings.
C) 1 of 4	This is the overall probability of being affected (aa) from a carrier × carrier cross. Not the carrier probability.
E) 3 of 4	This is the probability of being unaffected (AA or Aa) from the total cross. Not the carrier probability among unaffected.
IF autosomal recessive + unaffected sibling of affected individual → THEN 2/3 chance of being a carrier

72.stemSnippet: 45-year-old woman… crushing chest pain 10/10… pulse 136, systolic BP 70… ECG: ST elevation V1-V3, ST depression II/III/aVF… physician wants to increase BP WITHOUT increasing pulse. Drug class?

sections.title: Snapshot
sections.body:
45-year-old woman… crushing chest pain 10/10… pulse 136, systolic BP 70… ECG: ST elevation V1-V3, ST depression II/III/aVF… physician wants to increase BP WITHOUT increasing pulse. Drug class?

✅ Correct Answer: A) α-Adrenergic agonist

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Acute MI (ST elevation V1-V3 = anterior wall MI)

🔑 Cardiogenic shock (systolic BP 70, tachycardia 136)

🔑 Goal: ↑ BP without ↑ HR

🔑 α₁-adrenergic agonist (e.g., phenylephrine) → vasoconstriction → ↑ SVR → ↑ BP

🔑 Pure α₁ agonist does NOT increase heart rate (may actually cause reflex bradycardia)

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
B) α-Adrenergic antagonist	Would DECREASE BP (vasodilation). Opposite of what's needed.
C) β-Adrenergic agonist	Would increase HR (β₁ = chronotropy/inotropy). The question specifically says "without increasing pulse."
D) β-Adrenergic antagonist	Would decrease HR AND decrease BP (negative inotropy). Dangerous in cardiogenic shock.
E) Dopamine agonist	Dopamine at high doses has α effects (vasoconstriction) but also β₁ effects (↑ HR). Not a "pure" BP increase without HR increase.
IF need to ↑ BP without ↑ HR → THEN pure α₁-adrenergic agonist (phenylephrine)

B) Failure of normal kidney ascent	= Pelvic kidney. Kidney stays in pelvis but maintains normal shape. Not fused.
C) Failure of one ureteric bud to develop	= Renal agenesis (absent kidney). Would have ONE kidney, not a U-shaped fused kidney.

75.stemSnippet: 54-year-old woman… wants to lose weight… BMI 27… parents with T2DM… BP 140/90… fasting glucose 102. Compared to normal-weight woman, most likely serum abnormality?

sections.title: Snapshot
sections.body:
54-year-old woman… wants to lose weight… BMI 27… parents with T2DM… BP 140/90… fasting glucose 102. Compared to normal-weight woman, most likely serum abnormality?

✅ Correct Answer: D) Increased fasting insulin concentration

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Overweight (BMI 27) with metabolic syndrome features (HTN, impaired fasting glucose 102)

🔑 Family history of T2DM = genetic predisposition to insulin resistance

🔑 Obesity → insulin resistance → pancreas compensates by producing MORE insulin → hyperinsulinemia

🔑 Fasting glucose 102 = impaired fasting glucose (pre-diabetes) — insulin is keeping glucose barely controlled

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
A) Decreased cholesterol excretion	Obesity increases cholesterol synthesis but this isn't the most characteristic serum finding compared to hyperinsulinemia.
B) Decreased estrone concentration	Obesity INCREASES estrone (adipose tissue aromatizes androgens → estrone). Opposite direction.
C) Decreased leptin concentration	Obesity INCREASES leptin (more adipose tissue → more leptin). Obese patients have leptin RESISTANCE, not deficiency.
E) Increased growth hormone	Obesity DECREASES GH secretion. GH is suppressed in obesity.
F) Increased TSH	Obesity may mildly increase TSH, but this is not the most characteristic finding. Hyperinsulinemia is far more specific.
IF overweight/obese + pre-diabetes + family history T2DM → THEN insulin resistance → increased fasting insulin

76.stemSnippet: 17-year-old boy… 3 episodes of full-body weakness after football… resolves in 6 hours… eats "lots of pasta and salty foods" before playing… normal labs between episodes. Which serum concentration abnormal DURING an episode?

sections.title: Snapshot
sections.body:
17-year-old boy… 3 episodes of full-body weakness after football… resolves in 6 hours… eats "lots of pasta and salty foods" before playing… normal labs between episodes. Which serum concentration abnormal DURING an episode?

✅ Correct Answer: D) Potassium

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Episodic weakness after exercise = periodic paralysis

🔑 Triggered by high-carb meals ("pasta") + exercise → hypokalemic periodic paralysis

🔑 Carbohydrate load → insulin release → insulin drives K⁺ into cells → hypokalemia → muscle weakness

🔑 Resolves spontaneously in hours = classic for periodic paralysis

🔑 Normal labs between episodes = only abnormal DURING attacks

🧠 MULTI-STEP LOGIC

[Step 1] Episodic paralysis after carb-heavy meal + exercise

[Step 2] High carb intake → ↑ insulin secretion

[Step 3] Insulin → drives K⁺ intracellularly

[Step 4] Serum K⁺ drops → hypokalemia

[Step 5] Hypokalemia → muscle membrane hyperpolarization → weakness/paralysis

[Step 6] As insulin effect wears off → K⁺ normalizes → weakness resolves

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
A) Calcium	Hypocalcemia causes tetany/spasms (Chvostek, Trousseau), not episodic flaccid paralysis.
B) Chloride	Chloride abnormalities don't cause episodic paralysis.
C) Magnesium	Hypomagnesemia causes tremor, arrhythmias, seizures. Not episodic paralysis triggered by carbs.
E) Sodium	Hyponatremia causes confusion/seizures, not episodic muscle weakness triggered by carb intake.
IF episodic paralysis after carb-heavy meal → THEN hypokalemic periodic paralysis → abnormal potassium during episode

77.stemSnippet: 26-year-old man… 1-week increased urinary frequency + excessive thirst… urinating hourly… normal exam + normal serum chemistry… urine osmolality 50 mOsmol/kg… after ADH administration → urine osmolality normalizes. Dysfunction of which structure?

sections.title: Snapshot
sections.body:
26-year-old man… 1-week increased urinary frequency + excessive thirst… urinating hourly… normal exam + normal serum chemistry… urine osmolality 50 mOsmol/kg… after ADH administration → urine osmolality normalizes. Dysfunction of which structure?

✅ Correct Answer: F) Supraoptic nucleus

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Polyuria + polydipsia + dilute urine (50 mOsmol/kg) = diabetes insipidus (DI)

🔑 ADH administration → urine concentrates = kidneys RESPOND to ADH → this is CENTRAL DI (not nephrogenic)

🔑 Central DI = problem with ADH production/secretion

🔑 ADH is synthesized in the supraoptic nucleus (and paraventricular nucleus) of the hypothalamus

🔑 ADH is stored/released from the posterior pituitary but MADE in the hypothalamus

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
A) Anterior pituitary	Anterior pituitary produces GH, ACTH, TSH, FSH, LH, prolactin. NOT ADH.
B) Bowman capsule	Part of the glomerulus (filtration). Not involved in ADH production or water reabsorption regulation.
C) Glomerulus	Filtration structure. Glomerular disease causes proteinuria/hematuria, not DI.
D) Hypophysial portal system	Connects hypothalamus to ANTERIOR pituitary. ADH travels via the hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract to the POSTERIOR pituitary.
E) Loop of Henle	Creates the medullary concentration gradient. Loop dysfunction → inability to concentrate urine, but ADH would also not help (nephrogenic pattern). Here ADH DOES help → problem is ADH production.

✅ Correct Answer: D) Obstruction of bile flow

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia — direct bilirubin 14 out of total 20 = >50% direct = cholestatic jaundice

🔑 Dark urine = conjugated bilirubin excreted in urine (water-soluble)

🔑 Elevated liver enzymes (AST, ALT) + elevated GGT = cholestatic pattern

🔑 2-week-old with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia = biliary atresia until proven otherwise (most common cause of neonatal cholestasis requiring surgery)

🔑 Biliary atresia = obstruction of bile flow from progressive destruction/obliteration of extrahepatic bile ducts

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
A) Deficiency of UDP glucuronosyltransferase	= Gilbert syndrome or Crigler-Najjar. These cause UNCONJUGATED (indirect) hyperbilirubinemia. This patient has DIRECT hyperbilirubinemia.
B) Hemolysis	Hemolysis causes UNCONJUGATED hyperbilirubinemia (↑ indirect bilirubin). CBC is normal here. Direct bilirubin is elevated.
C) Low activity of bile canalicular MRP transporter	= Dubin-Johnson syndrome. Causes mild conjugated hyperbilirubinemia but NOT elevated liver enzymes or GGT. Benign condition.

✅ Correct Answer: D) 9992
🧠 MULTI-STEP LOGIC

[Step 1] Calculate test characteristics:

Sensitivity = 250/1000 = 25%

Specificity = 900/1000 = 90%

False positive rate = 1 - specificity = 10%

[Step 2] Apply to population of 100,000:

Prevalence = 80/100,000

Diseased = 80

Non-diseased = 100,000 - 80 = 99,920

[Step 3] False positives = Non-diseased × False positive rate

= 99,920 × 0.10

= 9,992 ✓

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
A) 20	This is the number of TRUE positives (80 × 0.25 = 20). Not false positives.
B) 80	This is the total number of diseased individuals. Not false positives.
C) 8993	Incorrect calculation — likely an arithmetic error or confusion with a different formula.
E) 10,012	This would be total positives (TP + FP = 20 + 9,992 = 10,012). Not just false positives.

✅ Correct Answer: E) Right parietal

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Left-sided neglect — walks into things on the LEFT, ignores left-sided stimuli

🔑 Extinction on double simultaneous stimulation (identifies right but not left when both presented) = classic hemispatial neglect

🔑 Left lower quadrantanopia = damage to upper optic radiations (parietal lobe)

🔑 No motor or language deficits = not frontal, not dominant temporal

🔑 Hemispatial neglect = RIGHT parietal lobe lesion (non-dominant hemisphere)

🧠 MULTI-STEP LOGIC

[Step 1] Left-sided neglect → RIGHT hemisphere lesion

(neglect is contralateral to lesion)

[Step 2] Extinction to double simultaneous stimulation → PARIETAL lobe

[Step 3] Left lower quadrantanopia → RIGHT parietal

(upper optic radiations in parietal lobe → contralateral lower quadrant)

[Step 4] No aphasia → confirms NON-DOMINANT (right) hemisphere

[Step 5] RIGHT PARIETAL lobe ✓

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
A) Left frontal	Left frontal → RIGHT-sided motor deficits + Broca aphasia. No neglect.
B) Left parietal	Left parietal → RIGHT-sided sensory loss + possible Gerstmann syndrome (dominant hemisphere). Neglect is rare with left-sided lesions.
C) Left temporal	Left temporal → Wernicke aphasia. No neglect.
D) Right frontal	Right frontal → LEFT-sided motor deficits. Neglect is possible but less classic than parietal. No motor deficits here.
F) Right temporal	Right temporal → LEFT upper quadrantanopia (Meyer's loop). This patient has LEFT LOWER quadrantanopia (parietal).
IF left-sided neglect + left lower quadrantanopia + no motor/language deficits → THEN right parietal lobe

84.stemSnippet: 75-year-old man… palpitations + lightheadedness + SOB + fatigue × 2 months… alcohol use disorder… recurrent pancreatitis… BMI 17… ECG shown. Abnormal electrical activity originating in which structure?

sections.title: Snapshot
sections.body:
75-year-old man… palpitations + lightheadedness + SOB + fatigue × 2 months… alcohol use disorder… recurrent pancreatitis… BMI 17… ECG shown. Abnormal electrical activity originating in which structure?

✅ Correct Answer: E) Right atrium

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Episodic palpitations + lightheadedness + SOB + fatigue = paroxysmal arrhythmia

🔑 Alcohol use disorder = major risk factor for atrial fibrillation ("holiday heart")

🔑 ECG likely shows atrial fibrillation (irregularly irregular rhythm, no P waves)

🔑 Atrial fibrillation = chaotic electrical activity originating in the atria

🔑 Most AF triggers originate from pulmonary vein ostia which empty into the left atrium, but the abnormal electrical activity involves BOTH atria

🔑 The answer key says right atrium — AF involves disorganized electrical activity throughout both atria, and the right atrium is listed as the answer

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
A) AV node	AV nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT) = regular, narrow-complex SVT. Not the irregularly irregular pattern of AF.
B) Bundle of His	His bundle pathology → heart block, not atrial arrhythmia.
C) Left ventricle	Ventricular origin → wide QRS complexes (VT). AF has narrow QRS (unless aberrant conduction).
D) Purkinje fibers	Purkinje pathology → ventricular arrhythmias. Not atrial.
F) Sinoatrial node	SA node pathology → sinus bradycardia, sinus arrest, sick sinus syndrome. Not the chaotic atrial activity of AF.
IF alcoholic + episodic palpitations + irregularly irregular rhythm → THEN atrial fibrillation → atrial origin

✅ Correct Answer: D) Inhibition of cyclooxygenase-1

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Oral ibuprofen = NSAID

🔑 Hematemesis + epigastric tenderness + guaiac positive stool = upper GI bleed from peptic ulcer/gastritis

🔑 NSAIDs cause GI damage by inhibiting COX-1 → decreased prostaglandin synthesis → decreased gastric mucosal protection

🔑 COX-1 produces prostaglandins (PGE₂) that:

↑ Mucus secretion

↑ Bicarbonate secretion

↑ Mucosal blood flow

↓ Acid secretion

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
A) Generation of nitric oxide	NO is gastroprotective (similar to prostaglandins). NSAIDs don't primarily work through NO inhibition.
B) Increased prostaglandin production	OPPOSITE — NSAIDs DECREASE prostaglandin production. That's the mechanism of GI harm.
C) Induction of pro-inflammatory cytokines	NSAIDs are anti-inflammatory. They don't cause GI damage through cytokine induction.
E) Pre-absorptive topical injury	This refers to direct mucosal irritation by the pill. While NSAIDs can cause local irritation, the PRIMARY mechanism of GI damage is SYSTEMIC COX-1 inhibition (even IV/rectal NSAIDs cause GI ulcers).
IF NSAID use + GI bleed → THEN COX-1 inhibition → decreased protective prostaglandins

86.stemSnippet: Male newborn at 38 weeks… oligohydramnios from uteroplacental insufficiency… small for gestational age… short feet pointing downward and turned inward (clubfoot). Disorder of development?

Male newborn at 38 weeks… oligohydramnios from uteroplacental insufficiency… small for gestational age… short feet pointing downward and turned inward (clubfoot). Disorder of development?

✅ Correct Answer: A) Deformation

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Oligohydramnios = decreased amniotic fluid

🔑 Clubfoot (talipes equinovarus) = feet turned inward/downward

🔑 Oligohydramnios → extrinsic mechanical compression on the fetus → deformation

🔑 Deformation = abnormal form/position caused by mechanical forces on a previously NORMAL structure

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
B) Disruption	Disruption = breakdown of a previously NORMAL structure (e.g., amniotic band syndrome). The feet were normal but compressed, not destroyed.
C) Dysplasia	Dysplasia = abnormal ORGANIZATION of cells within a tissue (e.g., thanatophoric dysplasia). This is a positional abnormality, not a cellular organization problem.
D) Malformation	Malformation = intrinsically abnormal developmental process (e.g., neural tube defect, heart septal defect). Clubfoot from oligohydramnios is EXTRINSIC compression, not an intrinsic developmental error.

✅ Correct Answer: B) Decreased fremitus, Hyperresonant percussion, Decreased breath sounds

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Penetrating chest trauma (knife wound to right chest)

🔑 Trachea shifted to the LEFT (AWAY from the right side) = tension pneumothorax

🔑 Tension pneumothorax = air trapped in pleural space → lung collapse + mediastinal shift

🧠 MULTI-STEP LOGIC

[Step 1] Knife wound → air enters pleural space → pneumothorax

[Step 2] Trachea shifts AWAY from affected side → TENSION pneumothorax

[Step 3] Right chest findings:

├─ Breath sounds: DECREASED (collapsed lung) ✓

├─ Percussion: HYPERRESONANT (air in pleural space) ✓

└─ Fremitus: DECREASED (no lung tissue transmitting vibrations) ✓

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
A) ↓ Fremitus, Dull, ↓ Breath sounds	Dullness = FLUID (pleural effusion or hemothorax). Pneumothorax = hyperresonant, not dull.
C) ↓ Fremitus, Hyperresonant, Dull	Mixed findings don't make sense — can't be hyperresonant AND dull simultaneously.
D) ↑ Fremitus, Dull, Bronchial	= Consolidation (pneumonia). Opposite of pneumothorax.
E) ↑ Fremitus, Dull, ↓ Breath sounds	Dullness with increased fremitus = consolidation. Decreased breath sounds with dullness = effusion. Neither fits pneumothorax.

88.stemSnippet: 22-year-old man… MVC with multiple lacerations… 20% blood loss… bleeding controlled in OR… peripheral blood smear in 10 days most likely shows?

sections.title: Snapshot
sections.body:
22-year-old man… MVC with multiple lacerations… 20% blood loss… bleeding controlled in OR… peripheral blood smear in 10 days most likely shows?

✅ Correct Answer: D) Polychromasia

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Acute blood loss (20% volume) → now controlled

🔑 10 days later = bone marrow has had time to respond

🔑 Bone marrow response to blood loss → increased erythropoiesis → release of reticulocytes

🔑 Reticulocytes on peripheral smear appear as polychromatic (bluish-gray) cells due to residual RNA

🔑 Polychromasia = presence of reticulocytes on Wright-stained smear

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
A) Heinz bodies	Heinz bodies = denatured hemoglobin (G6PD deficiency, oxidative stress). Not a response to blood loss.
B) Hypochromia	Hypochromia = iron deficiency (chronic blood loss). Acute blood loss with 10-day recovery → reticulocytosis, not iron deficiency yet.
C) Microspherocytosis	Microspherocytes = hereditary spherocytosis or autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Not a response to acute blood loss.
E) Siderotic granules	Siderotic granules (Pappenheimer bodies) = iron-laden mitochondria in sideroblastic anemia. Not related to acute blood loss recovery.
IF acute blood loss + 10 days recovery → THEN reticulocytosis → polychromasia on smear

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS

A) Magnesium	Magnesium deficiency → neuromuscular irritability, arrhythmias. Not dry scaly rash.
C) Vitamin B₁₂	B₁₂ deficiency → megaloblastic anemia + neurologic symptoms (subacute combined degeneration). Not dry scaly rash. B₁₂ is water-soluble.
D) Vitamin C	Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) → bleeding gums, petechiae, poor wound healing, corkscrew hairs. Not dry scaly rash. Water-soluble.
E) Zinc	Zinc deficiency → perioral/acral dermatitis (acrodermatitis enteropathica), dysgeusia, poor wound healing. Possible but vitamin A is more classic for dry scaly skin with fat malabsorption.

90.stemSnippet: 22-year-old woman with sickle cell disease… 3-day hematuria… no pain, no fever… CT: papillary necrosis. Which renal medullary findings increased risk?

sections.title: Snapshot
sections.body:
22-year-old woman with sickle cell disease… 3-day hematuria… no pain, no fever… CT: papillary necrosis. Which renal medullary findings increased risk?

✅ Correct Answer: C) Decreased oxygen tension, Increased osmolality

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Sickle cell disease + papillary necrosis

🔑 The renal medulla is uniquely vulnerable in sickle cell disease because of its environment:

Low oxygen tension (vasa recta countercurrent exchange → hypoxic medulla)

High osmolality (concentrated interstitium from countercurrent multiplication)

🔑 Both conditions promote sickling of RBCs → vascular occlusion → ischemic necrosis of the renal papilla

🧠 MULTI-STEP LOGIC

[Step 1] Renal medulla environment:

├─ LOW O₂ (vasa recta → countercurrent O₂ exchange)

├─ HIGH osmolality (up to 1200 mOsm/kg)

├─ LOW pH (acid secretion)

└─ LOW flow (sluggish vasa recta blood flow)

[Step 2] All of these promote HbS polymerization → sickling

[Step 3] Sickling → vascular occlusion → ischemia

[Step 4] Ischemia of renal papilla → PAPILLARY NECROSIS

[Step 5] Answer: ↓ O₂ tension + ↑ osmolality ✓

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
A) ↑ O₂, ↑ osmolality	Renal medulla has LOW O₂, not high. High O₂ would actually PREVENT sickling.
B) ↑ O₂, ↓ osmolality	Both wrong — medulla has low O₂ and high osmolality.
D) ↓ O₂, ↓ osmolality	O₂ is correct (low), but osmolality is HIGH in the medulla, not low.
IF sickle cell + papillary necrosis → THEN medullary environment (↓ O₂ + ↑ osmolality) promotes sickling

92.stemSnippet: 15-year-old boy… expelled from school for carrying knives… agitated, fearful, intermittently incoherent… upset since school shooting last week… "voice tells me I'll be hurt"… "dark eyes at night warn me"… "mother will stab me in my sleep"… normal labs, negative tox screen. sections.title: Snapshot
sections.body:
15-year-old boy… expelled from school for carrying knives… agitated, fearful, intermittently incoherent… upset since school shooting last week… "voice tells me I'll be hurt"… "dark eyes at night warn me"… "mother will stab me in my sleep"… normal labs, negative tox screen. Diagnosis?

✅ Correct Answer: B) Brief psychotic disorder

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Psychotic symptoms: auditory hallucinations ("voice tells me"), visual hallucinations ("dark eyes"), paranoid delusions ("mother will stab me")

🔑 Duration: symptoms began after school shooting last week = <1 month

🔑 Precipitating stressor: school shooting → identifiable stressor

🔑 Previously normal functioning ("He was fine before then, both at school and with his friends")

🔑 Negative tox screen = not substance-induced

🔑 Brief psychotic disorder = psychotic symptoms lasting 1 day to <1 month, often with identifiable stressor, with eventual full return to premorbid functioning

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
A) Adjustment disorder with anxiety	Adjustment disorder does NOT include psychotic symptoms (hallucinations, delusions). It involves emotional/behavioral symptoms (anxiety, depression) in response to a stressor.
C) PTSD	PTSD involves re-experiencing (flashbacks, nightmares), avoidance, hyperarousal. While triggered by trauma, PTSD does NOT typically include frank psychotic symptoms like command hallucinations and paranoid delusions. Also requires >1 month of symptoms.
D) Schizophrenia	Requires symptoms for ≥6 months (with ≥1 month of active-phase symptoms). This patient has had symptoms for 1 week. Also, premorbid functioning was normal.
E) Schizotypal personality disorder	Schizotypal = chronic pattern of odd beliefs, magical thinking, social awkwardness. NOT acute psychotic episodes. This patient was previously normal.

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 FEV₁/FVC = 1.0 (100%) = NOT obstructive (obstructive would be <0.7)

🔑 FEV₁ and FVC both severely reduced (26%) with normal ratio = RESTRICTIVE pattern

🔑 TLC 54% (reduced) = confirms restriction

🔑 DLCO 100% (NORMAL) = lung parenchyma is NORMAL → restriction is NOT from lung disease

🔑 RV 120% (elevated) = air trapping from weak expiratory muscles (can't fully exhale)

🔑 FRC 87% (relatively preserved) = chest wall at rest is normal

🔑 BMI 15 = severely cachectic/malnourished → muscle wasting

🔑 Age 85 + cachexia → respiratory muscle weakness (diaphragm, intercostals)

🔑 Hypercapnia (PCO₂ 48) = hypoventilation from weak muscles

🔑 Diaphragmatic excursion 1.5 cm (normal ≥5 cm) = weak diaphragm

🧠 MULTI-STEP LOGIC

[Step 1] FEV₁/FVC = 1.0 → NOT obstructive

[Step 2] ↓ FEV₁, ↓ FVC, ↓ TLC → RESTRICTIVE

[Step 3] DLCO = 100% (normal) → Lung parenchyma is FINE

→ Restriction is EXTRAPULMONARY

[Step 4] Extrapulmonary restriction + cachexia + ↑ RV:

→ Neuromuscular weakness ✓

[Step 5] ↑ PCO₂ (hypoventilation) confirms weak muscles

[Step 6] Decreased respiratory muscle strength ✓

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
A) Decreased lung elasticity	↓ Elasticity = emphysema → OBSTRUCTIVE pattern (↓ FEV₁/FVC). This patient has normal ratio.
C) Decreased surfactant production	↓ Surfactant → atelectasis (NRDS in neonates). Would cause ↓ DLCO. DLCO is normal here.
D) Increased alveolar surface tension	Same as surfactant deficiency. Would affect gas exchange → ↓ DLCO. DLCO is normal.
E) Increased bronchial mucous secretions	= Chronic bronchitis → OBSTRUCTIVE pattern. FEV₁/FVC would be 0.7.
F) Increased lung compliance	↑ Compliance = emphysema → OBSTRUCTIVE. This is restrictive.
🗺️ KEY CONCEPT

IF primary dysmenorrhea → THEN first-line = NSAIDs → inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis

✅ Correct Answer: D) Increased aquaporin expression

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Marathon runner in hot weather (90°F) → significant fluid/sweat losses

🔑 Dehydration (dry mucous membranes, ↓ skin turgor, hypotension, tachycardia)

🔑 Dehydration → ↑ serum osmolality → ↑ ADH release from posterior pituitary

🔑 ADH → binds V₂ receptors on collecting duct → inserts aquaporin-2 channels → ↑ water reabsorption

🔑 Increased aquaporin expression = kidney's compensatory response to conserve water

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
A) Decreased ADH receptors	Dehydration → ↑ ADH → if anything, receptors are UPREGULATED, not decreased. Decreased receptors = nephrogenic DI.
B) Decreased renin production	Dehydration → ↓ renal perfusion → INCREASED renin (RAAS activation). Opposite direction.
C) Decreased urine osmolality	Dehydration → kidneys CONCENTRATE urine → INCREASED urine osmolality. Opposite.
E) Increased GFR	Dehydration → ↓ renal perfusion → DECREASED GFR. Opposite.
F) Increased reabsorption of albumin	Albumin is not normally filtered (too large). Increased albumin reabsorption is not a normal compensatory response to dehydration.
IF dehydration → THEN ↑ ADH → ↑ aquaporin-2 insertion in collecting duct → water conservation

98.stemSnippet: 64-year-old man… metastatic melanoma… not surgically resectable… antibody blockade targeting which molecule provides most benefit?

sections.title: Snapshot
sections.body:
64-year-old man… metastatic melanoma… not surgically resectable… antibody blockade targeting which molecule provides most benefit?

✅ Correct Answer: D) CTLA4

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Metastatic melanoma — not resectable

🔑 Antibody blockade = immunotherapy (immune checkpoint inhibitor)

🔑 CTLA-4 = immune checkpoint receptor on T cells → sends INHIBITORY signal → turns OFF T-cell activation

🔑 Anti-CTLA-4 antibody (ipilimumab) = blocks the "off switch" → T cells remain activated → attack tumor

🔑 Ipilimumab was the first checkpoint inhibitor approved for metastatic melanoma

🧠 MULTI-STEP LOGIC

[Step 1] Metastatic melanoma, unresectable

→ Needs systemic therapy

[Step 2] Immunotherapy = standard of care for melanoma

[Step 3] Immune checkpoint inhibitors:

├─ Anti-CTLA-4 (ipilimumab) ✓

├─ Anti-PD-1 (nivolumab, pembrolizumab)

└─ Anti-PD-L1 (atezolizumab)

[Step 4] CTLA-4 normally inhibits T-cell activation

→ Blocking CTLA-4 → enhanced anti-tumor immunity ✓

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
A) B7	B7 (CD80/CD86) is on APCs → provides CO-STIMULATORY signal to T cells. Blocking B7 would SUPPRESS immunity (opposite of desired effect).
B) CD28	CD28 is the co-stimulatory receptor on T cells (binds B7). Blocking CD28 would SUPPRESS T-cell activation. Opposite of desired effect.
C) CD40	CD40 is on APCs → involved in APC activation. Blocking CD40 would impair immune activation. Not a checkpoint inhibitor target.
E) FcγR	Fc gamma receptors are on immune cells for antibody-mediated functions. Not a checkpoint target for melanoma immunotherapy.

101.stemSnippet: 25-year-old man… irritability, restlessness, tremor, palpitations × 4 hours… known amphetamine user… pulse 120, BP 150/100. Most likely cause = sympathomimetic activity from which mechanism?

sections.title: Snapshot
sections.body:
25-year-old man… irritability, restlessness, tremor, palpitations × 4 hours… known amphetamine user… pulse 120, BP 150/100. Most likely cause = sympathomimetic activity from which mechanism?

✅ Correct Answer: F) Increased release of biogenic amines

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Amphetamine use = sympathomimetic drug of abuse

🔑 Sympathetic overdrive: tachycardia (120), hypertension (150/100), tremor, restlessness, palpitations

🔑 Amphetamine mechanism: enters presynaptic nerve terminal → reverses VMAT and DAT/NET transporters → floods synaptic cleft with catecholamines (dopamine, norepinephrine, serotonin)

🔑 This is increased RELEASE of biogenic amines (not reuptake inhibition like cocaine)

🧠 MULTI-STEP LOGIC

[Step 1] Amphetamines enter presynaptic terminal via DAT/NET

[Step 2] Reverse vesicular monoamine transporter (VMAT)

→ monoamines leak from vesicles into cytoplasm

[Step 3] Reverse DAT/NET → monoamines pumped OUT into synapse

[Step 4] Net effect = MASSIVE RELEASE of NE, DA, 5-HT

[Step 5] Sympathomimetic symptoms ✓

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
A) Decreased intracellular metabolism of biogenic amines	This describes MAO inhibitors (prevent intracellular breakdown). Amphetamines have mild MAO inhibition but primary mechanism is RELEASE.
B) Decreased monoamine oxidase activity	Same as above — MAO inhibition is a minor component, not the primary mechanism.
C) Decreased presynaptic receptor activation	Decreased α₂ autoreceptor activation would increase NE release, but this isn't the mechanism of amphetamines.
D) Increased intracellular metabolism	Would DECREASE amines available. Opposite of what amphetamines do.
E) Increased presynaptic receptor activation	Increased α₂ activation would DECREASE NE release. Opposite effect.
🗺️ KEY DISTINCTION

║  AMPHETAMINES vs COCAINE                             ║

╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣

║                                                      ║

║  AMPHETAMINES ✓:                                     ║

║  ├─ RELEASE biogenic amines ✓                        ║

║  ├─ Reverse VMAT + DAT/NET                           ║

║  ├─ Also mild MAO inhibition                         ║

║  └─ Longer duration of action                        ║

║                                                      ║

║  COCAINE:                                            ║

║  ├─ BLOCKS REUPTAKE of biogenic amines               ║

║  ├─ Inhibits DAT, NET, SERT                          ║

║  ├─ Also blocks Na⁺ channels (local anesthetic)      ║

║  └─ Shorter duration of action                       ║

║                                                      ║

║  BOTH → ↑ synaptic catecholamines → sympathomimetic  ║

╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

IF amphetamine use + sympathomimetic symptoms → THEN increased release of biogenic amines

✅ Correct Answer: E) Stretched aortic anulus

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Very tall (6'5") young man = Marfan syndrome habitus

🔑 Severe upper back pain → aortic dissection (classic presentation)

🔑 Hypotension + tachycardia = hemorrhagic shock from dissection

🔑 Late diastolic murmur at LLSB = aortic regurgitation

🔑 Mechanism: aortic root dissection → dilation of the aortic root → stretching of the aortic annulus → aortic valve leaflets can't coapt → aortic regurgitation

🔑 Marfan syndrome → cystic medial necrosis → aortic root dilation → dissection

🧠 MULTI-STEP LOGIC

[Step 1] Tall young man → Marfan syndrome

[Step 2] Severe back pain + hemodynamic collapse → aortic dissection

[Step 3] Dissection involves aortic root → root dilates

[Step 4] Dilated root → aortic annulus stretches

[Step 5] Stretched annulus → valve leaflets don't close properly

[Step 6] → Aortic regurgitation (diastolic murmur at LLSB) ✓

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
A) Atrial septal defect	ASD → fixed split S2, systolic flow murmur at pulmonic area. NOT a diastolic murmur. Not associated with acute collapse.
B) Mitral stenosis	MS → low-pitched diastolic rumble at APEX (not LLSB). Associated with rheumatic heart disease, not Marfan.
C) Papillary muscle rupture	Papillary muscle rupture → acute MITRAL REGURGITATION (systolic murmur at apex). Not diastolic. Usually post-MI.
D) Perforated tricuspid valve	Tricuspid perforation → tricuspid regurgitation (systolic murmur at LLSB). Not diastolic. Associated with IV drug use/endocarditis.
IF tall young man + acute back pain + diastolic murmur at LLSB → THEN aortic dissection → stretched aortic annulus → aortic regurgitation

103.stemSnippet: 78-year-old woman with bronchogenic carcinoma… muscle weakness before operation… sevoflurane + pancuronium used… profound residual neuromuscular block postop… EPP amplitude 3 mV (normal 10), MEPP 1 mV (normal 1), ACh response 1 mV (normal 1). Most likely cause?

sections.title: Snapshot
sections.body:
78-year-old woman with bronchogenic carcinoma… muscle weakness before operation… sevoflurane + pancuronium used… profound residual neuromuscular block postop… EPP amplitude 3 mV (normal 10), MEPP 1 mV (normal 1), ACh response 1 mV (normal 1). Most likely cause?

✅ Correct Answer: E) Myasthenic (Lambert-Eaton) syndrome

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Bronchogenic carcinoma + muscle weakness = paraneoplastic syndrome

🔑 Profound residual neuromuscular block = exaggerated sensitivity to neuromuscular blockers

🔑 Electrophysiology:

EPP amplitude: 3 mV (↓↓ from normal 10) = decreased ACh RELEASE

MEPP amplitude: 1 mV (NORMAL) = each vesicle has normal ACh content

ACh response: 1 mV (NORMAL) = postsynaptic receptors are NORMAL

🔑 Interpretation: decreased number of vesicles released (↓ quantal content) but each vesicle is normal and receptors are normal → PRESYNAPTIC defect

🔑 Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) = antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels → decreased Ca²⁺ entry → decreased ACh vesicle release

🧠 MULTI-STEP LOGIC

[Step 1] ↓ EPP but normal MEPP and normal ACh response

→ Problem is QUANTITY of release, not vesicle content

or receptor function

[Step 2] = PRESYNAPTIC defect in vesicle release

[Step 3] Bronchogenic carcinoma + presynaptic defect

→ Lambert-Eaton syndrome ✓

[Step 4] Anti-VGCC antibodies → ↓ Ca²⁺ influx → ↓ ACh release

[Step 5] Exaggerated sensitivity to NMJ blockers ✓

C) Cholinergic crisis	Cholinergic crisis = excess ACh at NMJ (from anticholinesterase overdose). Would show INCREASED EPP, not decreased.
D) Myasthenia gravis	MG = antibodies against POSTSYNAPTIC ACh receptors. Would show ↓ MEPP amplitude AND ↓ ACh response (receptor blockade). Here both are NORMAL → not MG.

sections.title: Snapshot
sections.body:
28-year-old man… family members with abnormal calcium… asymptomatic… Ca²⁺ 11.3, PTH 112 (↑↑), urine calcium 42 mg/24h (LOW), fractional excretion of calcium <1%. Most likely cause = mutation of which receptor?

✅ Correct Answer: C) Calcium-sensing receptor

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Hypercalcemia (Ca 11.3) + elevated PTH (112) = hyperparathyroidism

🔑 LOW urine calcium (42 mg/24h) + fractional excretion <1% = kidneys are REABSORBING calcium excessively

🔑 Family history of abnormal calcium = familial condition

🔑 Asymptomatic — no stones, no fractures

🔑 This pattern = Familial Hypocalciuric Hypercalcemia (FHH)

🔑 FHH = inactivating mutation of the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR)

🔑 CaSR normally senses serum Ca²⁺ → when Ca²⁺ is high, CaSR signals parathyroid to STOP making PTH and signals kidney to EXCRETE calcium

🔑 Mutant CaSR → "thinks" calcium is LOW → continues PTH secretion + renal calcium reabsorption

🧠 MULTI-STEP LOGIC

[Step 1] Hypercalcemia + ↑ PTH → hyperparathyroidism

[Step 2] BUT urine calcium is LOW (<1% FECa)

→ NOT primary hyperparathyroidism

(1° HPT → HIGH urine calcium)

[Step 3] Family history + low urine calcium + ↑ PTH

→ Familial Hypocalciuric Hypercalcemia (FHH)

[Step 4] FHH = inactivating mutation of CaSR ✓

[Step 5] KEY: FHH is BENIGN — no treatment needed

(vs 1° HPT which may need parathyroidectomy)

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
A) Calcitonin gene-related peptide receptor	CGRP receptor is involved in vasodilation and migraine. Not related to calcium homeostasis in this context.
B) Calcitonin receptor	Calcitonin receptor is on osteoclasts. Calcitonin lowers calcium. Mutation wouldn't cause this specific pattern of ↑ PTH + low urine Ca.
D) PTH receptor	PTH receptor mutation → Jansen metaphyseal chondrodysplasia (activating) or pseudohypoparathyroidism (inactivating). Wouldn't cause ↑ PTH + low urine Ca pattern.
E) RANK	RANK is on osteoclast precursors. Involved in bone remodeling. Not related to this calcium-sensing feedback loop.
F) Vitamin D receptor	VDR mutation → vitamin D-resistant rickets. Not hypercalcemia with ↑ PTH.
🗺️ KEY DISTINCTION

║  HYPERCALCEMIA + ↑ PTH — TWO DIAGNOSES               ║

╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣

║  PRIMARY HYPERPARATHYROIDISM:                        ║

║  ├─ ↑ Ca²⁺, ↑ PTH                                   ║

║  ├─ ↑↑ Urine calcium (FECa >2%)                     ║

║  ├─ Usually sporadic (parathyroid adenoma)            ║

║  ├─ Symptomatic: stones, bones, groans, moans        ║

║  └─ Treatment: parathyroidectomy                     ║

║                                                      ║

║  FHH ✓:                                              ║

║  ├─ ↑ Ca²⁺, ↑ PTH (mild)                            ║

║  ├─ ↓ Urine calcium (FECa <1%) ✓                    ║

║  ├─ FAMILIAL (autosomal dominant) ✓                  ║

║  ├─ ASYMPTOMATIC ✓                                   ║

║  ├─ CaSR mutation ✓                                  ║

║  └─ Treatment: NONE (benign condition)               ║

║                                                      ║

║  KEY DIFFERENTIATOR: Urine calcium / FECa            ║

║  FECa >2% → 1° HPT                                  ║

║  FECa <1% → FHH ✓                                   ║

╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

IF hypercalcemia + ↑ PTH + LOW urine calcium (FECa <1%) + family history → THEN FHH → CaSR mutation

sections.title: Snapshot
sections.body:
3800-g newborn… vagina AND structure appearing as penis with urethra at base near vaginal opening… chromosomal analysis ordered. If karyotype is 46,XX, most likely cause?

✅ Correct Answer: C) Maternal androgen exposure

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Ambiguous genitalia — has both female and virilized structures

🔑 Karyotype 46,XX = genetic female

🔑 Virilization of a genetic female = excess androgens during development

🔑 The question specifies if karyotype is 46,XX — so we need a cause of virilization in a genetic female

🔑 Among the choices, maternal androgen exposure (exogenous androgens taken by mother during pregnancy) can virilize a 46,XX fetus

🧠 KEY DISTINCTION
🔑 Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency) is the MOST COMMON cause of ambiguous genitalia in 46,XX — but it's not listed as a choice

🔑 17α-hydroxyprogesterone deficiency (Choice A) would cause DECREASED androgens, not virilization

🔑 Among the available choices, maternal androgen exposure is the correct answer

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
A) 17α-Hydroxyprogesterone deficiency	17α-hydroxylase DEFICIENCY → ↓ cortisol, ↓ sex steroids → would cause UNDERVIRILIZATION in males, not virilization in females.
B) Increased müllerian-inhibiting substance	MIS (AMH) causes regression of müllerian ducts. In a 46,XX, increased MIS would cause absence of uterus/tubes but NOT virilization of external genitalia.
D) Presence of SRY gene	If SRY were present, the karyotype would effectively function as male. But the question states 46,XX — SRY is on the Y chromosome. If SRY translocated to X, the phenotype would be more fully male.
E) 5α-Reductase deficiency	5α-reductase deficiency affects 46,XY individuals (undervirilized males). In a 46,XX individual, there's no significant testosterone to convert, so this enzyme deficiency is irrelevant.
IF 46,XX + virilized external genitalia → THEN excess androgen exposure (maternal source or CAH)

108.stemSnippet: 27-year-old woman… 2-week double vision… left eye does not adduct past midline on rightward gaze… leftward gaze is normal. Damage to which structure?

sections.title: Snapshot
sections.body:
27-year-old woman… 2-week double vision… left eye does not adduct past midline on rightward gaze… leftward gaze is normal. Damage to which structure?

✅ Correct Answer: B) Left medial longitudinal fasciculus

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Left eye cannot ADDUCT when looking RIGHT = internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO)

🔑 Leftward gaze is normal = left eye can abduct normally

🔑 INO = damage to the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF)

🔑 The MLF on the LEFT side connects the RIGHT CN VI nucleus to the LEFT CN III nucleus

🔑 When LEFT MLF is damaged → signal from RIGHT CN VI nucleus cannot reach LEFT CN III → LEFT eye fails to adduct on rightward gaze

🧠 MULTI-STEP LOGIC

[Step 1] Looking RIGHT:

├─ RIGHT eye abducts (CN VI — works ✓)

└─ LEFT eye should adduct (CN III via MLF)

→ FAILS to adduct ✗

[Step 2] The signal pathway for leftward adduction:

RIGHT CN VI nucleus → LEFT MLF → LEFT CN III nucleus

→ LEFT medial rectus → adduction

[Step 3] LEFT MLF is damaged ✓

→ Signal can't reach LEFT CN III

→ LEFT eye can't adduct on rightward gaze

[Step 4] Leftward gaze is normal because:

LEFT CN VI nucleus → RIGHT MLF (intact) → RIGHT CN III

→ RIGHT medial rectus adducts normally

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
A) Left abducens nerve	Left CN VI damage → left eye can't ABDUCT (not adduct). Leftward gaze would be impaired, not rightward.
C) Left nucleus of abducens nerve	Same as above — CN VI nucleus damage → impaired ABDUCTION of ipsilateral eye.
D) Right abducens nerve	Right CN VI damage → right eye can't abduct. But right eye abducts normally here.
E) Right MLF	Right MLF damage → RIGHT eye can't adduct on LEFTWARD gaze. But leftward gaze is normal here.
F) Right nucleus of abducens nerve	Right CN VI nucleus damage → right eye can't abduct AND (via MLF) left eye can't adduct. But this would affect BOTH eyes on rightward gaze.

110.stemSnippet: 16-day-old male newborn… 2-day jaundice + dark urine… born at 36 weeks… breast-feeding well… total bilirubin 20, DIRECT 14 mg/dL… ↑ ALP, ↑ AST, ↑ ALT, ↑ GGT. Most likely underlying cause?

sections.title: Snapshot
sections.body:
16-day-old male newborn… 2-day jaundice + dark urine… born at 36 weeks… breast-feeding well… total bilirubin 20, DIRECT 14 mg/dL… ↑ ALP, ↑ AST, ↑ ALT, ↑ GGT. Most likely underlying cause?

✅ Correct Answer: D) Obstruction of bile flow

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia — direct bilirubin 14/20 = 70% direct

🔑 Dark urine = conjugated bilirubin excreted in urine (water-soluble)

🔑 Elevated GGT = biliary obstruction marker

🔑 Elevated ALP, AST, ALT = cholestatic/hepatocellular injury pattern

🔑 16-day-old with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia = ALWAYS PATHOLOGIC (never physiologic)

🔑 Neonatal conjugated hyperbilirubinemia + elevated GGT = think biliary atresia (most common cause of neonatal cholestasis requiring surgery)

🔑 Biliary atresia = obstruction of extrahepatic bile ducts → bile can't flow → cholestasis

🧠 MULTI-STEP LOGIC

[Step 1] Jaundice at 16 days → prolonged jaundice (>2 weeks)

[Step 2] DIRECT hyperbilirubinemia (14 mg/dL) → CONJUGATED

→ NOT physiologic jaundice (which is unconjugated)

[Step 3] Dark urine → conjugated bilirubin in urine

[Step 4] ↑ GGT + ↑ ALP → CHOLESTATIC pattern

[Step 5] Neonatal cholestasis with ↑ GGT → biliary atresia

(vs Alagille, choledochal cyst, etc.)

[Step 6] Mechanism = OBSTRUCTION OF BILE FLOW ✓

❌ DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS
Choice	Why It's Wrong
A) Deficiency of UDP glucuronosyltransferase	UGT deficiency = Crigler-Najjar or Gilbert syndrome → UNCONJUGATED (indirect) hyperbilirubinemia. This patient has DIRECT hyperbilirubinemia.
B) Hemolysis	Hemolysis → ↑ UNCONJUGATED bilirubin + anemia + reticulocytosis. CBC is normal here. Bilirubin is predominantly DIRECT.
C) Low activity of bile canalicular MRP transporter	MRP2 deficiency = Dubin-Johnson syndrome → conjugated hyperbilirubinemia BUT with NORMAL liver enzymes and NORMAL GGT. This patient has elevated GGT/ALP/AST/ALT → obstruction, not transporter deficiency.
🗺️ KEY DISTINCTION

╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗

╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣

║  ├─ Physiologic jaundice (days 2-5, resolves by 2wk) ║

║  ├─ Breast milk jaundice (weeks 2-12)                ║

║  ├─ Hemolysis (ABO/Rh incompatibility, G6PD)         ║

║  ├─ Crigler-Najjar (UGT deficiency)                  ║

║  └─ Gilbert syndrome                                 ║

║                                                      ║

║  CONJUGATED (direct) ✓ — ALWAYS PATHOLOGIC:          ║

║  ├─ Biliary atresia ✓ (most common surgical cause)   ║

║  │   ├─ ↑ GGT ✓                                     ║

║  │   ├─ Acholic (pale) stools                        ║

║  │   ├─ Dark urine ✓                                 ║

║  │   └─ Kasai procedure needed by 60 days            ║

║  ├─ Choledochal cyst                                 ║

║  ├─ [Alagille syndrome](/rare-disease/alagille-syndrome)                                ║

║  ├─ Neonatal hepatitis                               ║

║  └─ TORCH infections                                 ║

╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

IF neonate + conjugated hyperbilirubinemia + dark urine + ↑ GGT → THEN obstruction of bile flow (biliary atresia)

sections.title: 🔑 HIGHLIGHTED VIGNETTE CLUES
sections.body:
🔑 Young woman (21 years old)

🔑 Severe hypertension (220/100) = secondary hypertension

🔑 Abdominal bruit = renal artery stenosis

🔑 LVH on ECG = chronic severe HTN → cardiac remodeling

🔑 Normal renal function (normal BUN/Cr) = early disease, kidney not yet damaged

🔑 Young woman + renal artery stenosis = fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD)
